summary: Lomustine (CCNU) is an oral lipophilic nitrosourea alkylating agent used for primary and metastatic brain tumours following surgery and/or radiotherapy, and as part of combination chemotherapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma that has progressed after initial therapy. It carries a BOXED WARNING for delayed, dose-related, cumulative myelosuppression (occurring 4-6 weeks after a dose, with thrombocytopenia usually more severe than leukopenia) and for fatal toxicity with overdosage - so it must be given as a SINGLE oral dose only once every 6 weeks, and only enough capsules for one dose should ever be prescribed or dispensed. The recommended dose is 130 mg/m2 as a single oral dose every 6 weeks (reduced to 100 mg/m2 with compromised marrow), with dose modifications based on the haematologic nadir. Other risks include pulmonary fibrosis, secondary malignancies (leukaemia/myelodysplasia), hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity.
indications: Primary and metastatic brain tumours following appropriate surgical and/or radiotherapeutic procedures
Hodgkin's lymphoma, as a component of combination chemotherapy, after disease progression on initial chemotherapy

admin: PRESCRIBE, DISPENSE AND ADMINISTER ONLY ENOUGH CAPSULES FOR ONE DOSE - never dispense the whole container (fatal overdose risk)
Give as a single oral dose every 6 weeks; the dose may combine capsules of different strengths/colours (10, 40, 100 mg)
Take on an empty stomach (e.g. at bedtime, no food for several hours) to reduce nausea and vomiting; consider antiemetic premedication
Do not break or open capsules; wear impervious gloves when handling and wash skin immediately if contact occurs (cytotoxic)
Monitor blood counts weekly for at least 6 weeks after each dose because myelosuppression is delayed
Reinforce to the patient that only one dose is taken every 6 weeks
moa: Lomustine is a lipid-soluble nitrosourea. After metabolic activation it generates alkylating and carbamoylating intermediates: the alkylating moiety crosslinks and modifies DNA (and RNA), inhibiting DNA synthesis and repair, while the carbamoylating moiety modifies proteins and further impairs DNA repair enzymes. These actions are cell-cycle non-specific and cytotoxic to dividing cells. Its high lipophilicity and lack of ionisation allow it to cross the blood-brain barrier readily, making it useful against CNS tumours.

absolute: None listed in the FDA label (relative cautions apply)
relative: Recent other myelosuppressive chemotherapy or radiotherapy
monitor: Complete blood counts weekly for at least 6 weeks after each dose
Pulmonary function tests at baseline and frequently
Liver aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin

preg: Lomustine can cause fetal harm based on its mechanism and animal data (embryotoxicity, teratogenicity). Advise women of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during and for an interval after treatment, and men with female partners likewise. Avoid in pregnancy unless the maternal benefit clearly outweighs fetal risk.
lact: Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed infant, women should not breastfeed during treatment with lomustine and for at least 2 weeks after the final dose.
renal: Lomustine can cause nephrotoxicity and progressive renal failure, particularly with prolonged therapy and high cumulative doses. Monitor renal function; use with caution and consider dose reduction in patients with renal impairment.
hepatic: Lomustine can elevate transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin and cause hepatotoxicity. Monitor liver function tests; use with caution in hepatic impairment.

major: Other myelosuppressive chemotherapy or radiotherapy - additive, potentially severe and prolonged bone-marrow suppression; reduce dose
Live vaccines - risk of severe/fatal infection in the immunosuppressed; avoid
moderate: Cimetidine - reported to enhance lomustine-induced myelotoxicity
Phenobarbital - may reduce lomustine efficacy via enhanced metabolism
Anticoagulants - bleeding risk increased with thrombocytopenia
Other hepatotoxic or nephrotoxic drugs - additive organ toxicity

interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive nausea and hepatic stress
interactions.diagnostics: May lower blood counts and raise LFTs; monitor CBC, LFTs and renal function

counsel: Take this medicine as a single dose only - NEVER take more than the one dose your team gives you; an extra dose can be fatal
It is given only once every 6 weeks; do not repeat it sooner
Take it on an empty stomach to lessen nausea; you may be given anti-sickness medicine
Blood counts fall weeks after the dose, so you will need regular blood tests - report fever, sore throat, unusual bruising or bleeding at once
Use reliable contraception and do not breastfeed during and after treatment
Report any new cough or breathlessness, as this drug can affect the lungs
pk: Rapidly absorbed; metabolites appear in plasma within minutes of an oral dose
Active metabolites peak within about 1-4 hours; crosses into CSF
Myelosuppressive effect is delayed (nadir 4-6 weeks) and cumulative
Store at controlled room temperature; keep capsules in original container, protect from heat; dispense only one dose
pearls: BOXED WARNING: delayed, cumulative myelosuppression (nadir 4-6 weeks; thrombocytopenia > leukopenia) and fatal overdose risk - dispense ONLY one dose
Give as a single oral dose no more often than every 6 weeks; monitor CBC weekly for >=6 weeks after each dose
Highly lipophilic, crosses the blood-brain barrier - hence its role in brain tumours
Watch for cumulative pulmonary fibrosis and nephrotoxicity with repeated/high cumulative doses
Secondary leukaemia/myelodysplasia can follow long-term use
missed: Lomustine is given as a single supervised dose every 6 weeks, so routine self-managed missed doses do not apply. If a scheduled dose is delayed, your oncology team will reschedule it - never take an extra or earlier dose, as overdose can be fatal.
overdose: Overdose causes fatal toxicity, chiefly profound and prolonged bone-marrow aplasia, severe gastrointestinal toxicity, hepatic and pulmonary injury. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive and intensive: monitor and support blood counts (transfusions, growth factors), treat infections aggressively, and provide organ support. The boxed warning stresses dispensing only one dose to prevent accidental overdose.
